conbody.p: Claimants who act in the opportunistic and exploitative manner known as “trolling” must be deterred and perhaps punished in some way. In order to do so, a definition for what counts as “copyright trolling” must first be created. Sag asserts this as a remedy to the issue of copyright abuse in his article, providing a rough definition: the essence of trolling is that the plaintiff is more focused on the business of litigation than on selling a product or service. The…troll plays a numbers game in which it targets hundreds or thousands of defendants, seeking quick settlements. While tightening guidelines of MDJD litigation and lowering the cap on statutory damages will likely deter this behavior, it is possible that holders may still seek to use copyright litigation as an independent revenue stream. Close attention to the character of claimants should be paid and repeat claimants, particularly those who have favored MDJD litigation in the past, should be questioned. If found to remain a prevalent issue following the adjustment of MDJD guidelines and decreased damages, disciplinary action in the form of the removal of an abusive claimant’s copyright or a fine can be implemented to further deter such abuse.
